The eruption of Mount Pelée on the French Caribbean island of Martinique, which on 8 May 1902 destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre and killed nearly all of its roughly 28,000 people in a few minutes. It was the deadliest volcanic eruption of the 20th century.

The volcano had rumbled for weeks, and a mudflow had killed workers at a sugar mill. Officials did not order an evacuation, perhaps partly because an election was due days later.

That morning a glowing cloud of hot gas, ash and rock rushed down the mountain and swept over the town and the ships in its harbour. One of the few survivors, Ludger Sylbaris, was a prisoner in a thick-walled cell.

The French scientist Alfred Lacroix studied the eruption, and such avalanches of hot gas and ash are now called pyroclastic flows. A day earlier the Soufrière volcano on nearby Saint Vincent had also erupted, killing over a thousand people. Saint-Pierre was never fully rebuilt.
